ocar.opportunity: Chimera states—coexistence of synchronized and desynchronized activity—are a candidate dynamical motif for modular brains, but they had been studied mainly in non-modular complex networks.
ocar.challenge: It was unclear whether a biologically inspired modular graph, with different synapse types inside versus between communities, could produce chimera-like dynamics rather than global synchrony or metastable chaos.
ocar.action: Hizanidis, Kouvaris, Zamora-López, Díaz-Guilera, and Antonopoulos, in Scientific Reports (2015; arXiv extract), simulate chaotic bursting neurons on a C. elegans–inspired network of six communities, with electrical coupling inside communities and chemical coupling across them, and score coherence with the Kuramoto order parameter ρ plus chimera-like χ and metastability λ indices.
ocar.resolution: Coaction of the two coupling types can produce chimera-like states: larger communities synchronize while smaller ones desynchronize. In the (gch, gel) plane, a high-χ / low-λ edge (illustrated at gch = 0.015, gel = 0.5) separates globally synchronous from highly metastable regimes. Similar behavior appears in networks that share features with the C. elegans graph.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the phenomenon as potentially informative for more complex modular brains; living-animal physiology is not tested here.

summaries.beginner: In a computer model inspired by the worm’s wiring, some groups of cells fire together while others fire out of step. That mixed pattern, called a chimera-like state, appears when local electrical coupling and longer-range chemical coupling are balanced just so.
summaries.intermediate: Hizanidis and colleagues (Scientific Reports, 2015) place chaotic bursting neurons on a six-community network inspired by the C. elegans connectome, with electrical synapses within communities and chemical synapses between them. Besides the Kuramoto order parameter, they use a chimera-like index χ (synchronization differences among communities) and a metastability index λ (variation over time). Parameter-space maps show a chimera-like regime on the boundary between globally synchronous and desynchronized/metastable dynamics, illustrated at gch = 0.015, gel = 0.5, where some communities lock and others do not. Analogous modular graphs behave similarly under the same assumptions.
summaries.advanced: This is a numerical study of a C. elegans–inspired modular graph, not a claim about living worms. The supplied extract is arXiv:1510.00286v2 of the Scientific Reports paper. Figure 3’s 1–277 neuron index should not be treated as a new biological census. Chimera-like here is defined by high χ and low λ, not by a unique biological mechanism.

plain_language_summary: In a computer model inspired by the worm’s wiring, some groups of cells fire together while others fire out of step. That mixed pattern, called a chimera-like state, appears when local electrical coupling and longer-range chemical coupling are balanced just so.

ocar.opportunity: Human macroconnectomics increasingly treats the number of reconstructed diffusion streamlines (NOS) as a stand-in for cortico-cortical projection strength. A cross-species check against gold-standard tract tracing would say how realistic that metric is.
ocar.challenge: The link between in vivo DWI NOS and invasive measures of anatomical connectivity strength in the same species remained poorly quantified, and deterministic tracking is known to over- and under-represent classes of tracts.
ocar.action: van den Heuvel and colleagues, in Human Brain Mapping (2015), compare GQI tractography from high-angular DWI in 10 rhesus macaques (600 directions total) with projection-strength tables from CoCoMac and the Markov–Kennedy high-resolution tract-tracing dataset.
ocar.resolution: NOS and streamline density correlated positively with tract-tracing strength in both datasets (both P < 0.001), with the clearest relationships after log transformation. NOS was the strongest DWI correlate; radial or mean diffusivity added unique variance in a combined model, whereas FA did not. The authors treat reconstructed streamline counts as a useful approximation of axonal number for in vivo DWI connectomes.
ocar.future_work: The discussion notes that the biological meaning of lognormal connectivity-strength distributions is still unclear, and that systematic under- and over-representation of tract classes remains a limit of deterministic fiber tracking.

summaries.beginner: MRI maps of brain cables are cheaper than injecting tracers, but it is hard to know whether more reconstructed fibers really mean a stronger connection. In macaques, streamline counts from diffusion MRI do rise with classic tracer measures of pathway strength.
summaries.intermediate: van den Heuvel et al. (Human Brain Mapping, 2015) compare DWI-derived number of streamlines (NOS) and streamline density from 10 rhesus macaques with CoCoMac and Markov–Kennedy tract-tracing weights. High-quality GQI data (600 directions in total) yield positive associations with tracer strength in both databases (P < 0.001), strongest for log-transformed values. A multilinear model with NOS plus RD (or MD) explained more CoCoMac variance than NOS alone (factor 1.39 for NOS+RD). FA was not a clear correlate. The paper argues that in vivo DWI connectomes can give fairly realistic estimates of white-matter projection strength.
summaries.advanced: Association is statistical, not proof that NOS equals axon count. Deterministic tracking biases (long-range over/under-representation) are acknowledged. The 1.39 factor is for a CoCoMac NOS+RD model versus NOS alone. PDF is a Europe PMC/Human Brain Mapping typeset copy. Species is rhesus macaque, not human.

plain_language_summary: MRI maps of brain cables are cheaper than injecting tracers, but it is hard to know whether more reconstructed fibers really mean a stronger connection. In macaques, streamline counts from diffusion MRI do rise with classic tracer measures of pathway strength.

ocar.opportunity: If a connectome is a complete map of anatomical and functional connectivity, glia belong in it: they shape wiring and signaling from whole-brain white matter down to individual synapses.
ocar.challenge: Connectomics has been framed almost exclusively around neurons, even though astrocytes, microglia, and oligodendrocytes operate on different spatial and temporal scales and use partly shared transmitter systems.
ocar.action: Fields, Woo, and Basser, in a Neuron (2015) Perspective, review glial contributions to long-range networks, local circuits, and synapses, including myelination, metabolic support, blood-flow coupling, and synapse pruning.
ocar.resolution: They argue that all major glial classes influence structural and functional connectivity, that myelin both speeds long-range communication and restricts axonal sprouting, and that glial computation is not well captured by neuronal membrane-potential models. A neuronal-only map is therefore incomplete.
ocar.future_work: The piece closes by rejecting the idea that glial structure and function will fall out automatically from neuronal connectomes; multicellular analysis is required.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram of the brain is usually a map of neurons. This essay argues that support cells—glia—also shape those wires, from whole-brain pathways down to single synapses, so they belong in the connectome too.
summaries.intermediate: Fields, Woo, and Basser (Neuron, 2015) write a Perspective that astrocytes, microglia, and oligodendrocytes should be part of any complete connectome. They survey glial effects on long-range networks (myelination, conduction-time inference from path length and axon diameter), local circuits, and synapses (pruning, neuromodulatory factors). Glia share transmitter-based signaling with neurons but operate on different morphological and temporal scales. The authors warn against assuming glial roles will be revealed as a byproduct of tracing neurons alone.
summaries.advanced: This is a perspective, not a new reconstruction. Conduction-time inference from dMRI path length plus axon-diameter distributions is a proposed measurement strategy, not a delivered atlas. Calcium imaging’s prominence in glial signaling is treated as a methods bias. The extract’s latter pages enter the reference list.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram of the brain is usually a map of neurons. This essay argues that support cells—glia—also shape those wires, from whole-brain pathways down to single synapses, so they belong in the connectome too.

ocar.opportunity: A mesoscale whole-brain axonal projection atlas of the mouse is only as useful as the informatics that put raw injections into a common 3D space and turn signal into quantitative connection strengths.
ocar.challenge: Meaningful comparison of connectome data depends on a high-fidelity atlas template, precise mapping of raw datasets, accurate signal detection, quantitative strength algorithms, and an integrated public interface.
ocar.action: Kuan, Li, Lau, Feng, Bernard, Sunkin, Zeng, Dang, Hawrylycz, and Ng, in Methods (2015), as described in the catalog abstract, describe key informatics pipeline steps behind the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas of the C57Bl/6J mouse.
ocar.resolution: The abstract presents a standardized platform that maps anatomical trajectories into a common 3D space, yielding a quantitative database of inter-areal and cell-type-specific projections with brain-wide coverage, a single data format, and open access at connectivity.brain-map.org, plus basic application use cases.
ocar.future_work: How later pipeline revisions changed quantification is outside the abstract.

summaries.beginner: The Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas is a public 3D map of which mouse brain areas send axons where. This methods paper explains the computer pipeline that turns injection images into that quantitative atlas.
summaries.intermediate: Kuan and colleagues (Methods, 2015) describe informatics for the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas, a mesoscale axonal-projection resource for the C57Bl/6J mouse. Per the catalog abstract, trajectories are mapped into a common 3D template to produce a quantitative, cell-type-aware projection database with brain-wide coverage and a public interface (http://connectivity.brain-map.org/). The paper’s stated focus is pipeline steps—template, registration, signal detection, strength quantification, and online presentation—plus basic use cases. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Bergmans and Celikel, Network Neuroscience, on NeuroCarta, an open-source MATLAB toolbox for building graphs from the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas, not the Kuan et al. Methods informatics paper. Claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of the 2015 Methods article is required for pipeline algorithms and validation.

plain_language_summary: The Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas is a public 3D map of which mouse brain areas send axons where. This methods paper explains the computer pipeline that turns injection images into that quantitative atlas.

ocar.opportunity: Finding which nodes actually matter in directed biological networks—command neurons, global regulators, conserved non-hubs—would give control and pharmacology targets that degree or PageRank can miss.
ocar.challenge: Most importance metrics were developed for undirected graphs; directed biological networks have motif structure (e.g. feed-forward loops) that those scores ignore.
ocar.action: Wang, Lü, and Yu, in PLoS ONE (2014), combine network-motif participation with principal component analysis to rank nodes, and test the index on five real directed biological networks (a neural network, three transcriptional regulatory networks, and a signal-transduction network).
ocar.resolution: The measure recovers biologically important nodes, including command interneurons and non-hub but conserved regulators. ROC curves on the five networks are reported as showing high prediction accuracy. If the feed-forward loop is the only motif, the index reduces to existing motif centrality.
ocar.future_work: The authors note computational cost if more motif types are included, and they propose extensions to electrical and social networks; finding still more effective node features remains open.

summaries.beginner: Not every important cell in a directed biological network is a hub with many links. This paper scores nodes by the wiring triangles they sit in, and reports that the score finds command neurons and key regulators better than simpler rankings.
summaries.intermediate: Wang, Lü, and Yu (PLoS ONE, 2014) introduce a motif-plus-PCA importance index for directed biological networks. They evaluate it on five real networks of different sizes and densities: one neural, three transcriptional, and one signal-transduction. They report recovery of command interneurons, global regulators, and conserved non-hub nodes, with ROC analysis described as high-accuracy. The method is offered as an alternative to degree, betweenness, and PageRank. Including more motif types raises computational complexity; unique FFL structure collapses the index to motif centrality.
summaries.advanced: ‘Very high prediction accuracy’ is the authors’ ROC summary, not a single AUC quoted in the extract. Ground-truth ‘important’ labels are network-specific biological annotations. The paper is a methods-and-application study across mixed biological graphs, not a new connectome. Editor was Mark D. McDonnell.

plain_language_summary: Not every important cell in a directed biological network is a hub with many links. This paper scores nodes by the wiring triangles they sit in, and reports that the score finds command neurons and key regulators better than simpler rankings.

ocar.opportunity: Many systems, including neuronal connectomes, are multilayer: several relationship types among the same entities. Analysis and visualization tools for that representation were scarce.
ocar.challenge: Without software that jointly handles interlayer structure, spatial overlays, and standard graph diagnostics, multilayer data are flattened into misleading single-layer graphs.
ocar.action: De Domenico, Porter, and Arenas, in Journal of Complex Networks (2015 version of a 2014 paper; arXiv:1405.0843), present muxViz, an open-source package of multilayer algorithms with interactive visualization, demonstrated on genetic, neuronal, and transportation networks.
ocar.resolution: The software is shown on a C. elegans connectome and on Herpes simplex and HIV-1 genetic-interaction networks, including centrality and other diagnostics (eigenvector centrality is omitted on a DAG layer). Code is released at github.com/manlius/muxViz.
ocar.future_work: The paper is a methods/software demonstration; new biological discoveries are not the claim.

summaries.beginner: Some networks have more than one kind of link between the same players, like different synapse types. This paper releases muxViz, a free tool to analyze and draw those multilayer maps, including a worm nervous-system example.
summaries.intermediate: De Domenico, Porter, and Arenas (J. Complex Networks / arXiv, 2014–2015) introduce muxViz for multilayer network analysis and interactive visualization. The abstract and extract demonstrate genetic, neuronal, and transportation examples; figure panels walk through a C. elegans connectome and Herpes simplex and HIV-1 genetic-interaction networks. The tool can overlay spatial information. Software is at https://github.com/manlius/muxViz. The catalog title omits the MuxViz prefix used on the arXiv PDF, but it is the same paper.
summaries.advanced: This is a software paper; C. elegans and viral-genetic figures are illustrations, not new reconstructions. Eigenvector centrality is skipped on a directed acyclic layer. The extract’s ‘discussion’ is brief and then figure captions. Treat the GitHub repo, not this PDF, as the current feature list.

plain_language_summary: Some networks have more than one kind of link between the same players, like different synapse types. This paper releases muxViz, a free tool to analyze and draw those multilayer maps, including a worm nervous-system example.

ocar.opportunity: Block-face SEM now yields large, nearly isotropic stacks and many automated segmentations, but measuring the 3D geometry of spines and boutons still lagged the reconstruction tools.
ocar.challenge: Few packages let a user view meshes together with the original EM stack, manipulate objects in 3D, and take morphometric measurements on arbitrary subregions without returning to slow manual tracing.
ocar.action: Jorstad, Nigro, Calì, Wawrzyniak, Fua, and Knott, in Neuroinformatics (2015 of a 2014 paper), release NeuroMorph, a Blender add-on for viewing segmentations with the source stack and collecting morphometric measurements.
ocar.resolution: The toolkit is presented as a faster path from computer-vision meshes to shape measurements of dendritic spines and axonal boutons. Code is open source (GNU GPL; RRID:SciRes_000156) at cvlab.epfl.ch/NeuroMorph, with example meshes and documentation; Blender is RRID:nif-0000-31943.
ocar.future_work: The paper positions NeuroMorph as bridging automated reconstruction and quantitative ultrastructure; it is not itself a connectome.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope stacks can be turned into 3D cell shapes, but measuring those shapes is still tedious. NeuroMorph is a free add-on to the Blender 3D program that lets you inspect and measure spines and boutons on those models.
summaries.intermediate: Jorstad and colleagues (Neuroinformatics, 2015) describe NeuroMorph, a Blender toolset for morphometric analysis of 3D models from serial EM, motivated by block-face SEM’s large, near-isotropic stacks. Users view segmentation results with the original image stack, manipulate objects, and measure arbitrary regions, aiming to speed geometry collection on dendritic spines and axonal boutons. The code is GNU GPL at cvlab.epfl.ch/NeuroMorph. The paper is a software original article, not a circuit reconstruction.
summaries.advanced: Catalog year is 2014; the PDF is Neuroinform (2015) 13:83–92. RRIDs are those stated. No accuracy benchmark versus manual stereology is in the selected extract. SBF-SEM appears among catalog methods; the tool is reconstruction-agnostic in the text.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope stacks can be turned into 3D cell shapes, but measuring those shapes is still tedious. NeuroMorph is a free add-on to the Blender 3D program that lets you inspect and measure spines and boutons on those models.

ocar.opportunity: Individual human MRI connectomes differ, but edges that recur across many subjects could serve as a lower-noise reference graph of the cortex.
ocar.challenge: There is no single ‘graph of the brain,’ so users need a parameterized way to keep only consensus edges and to download anatomically labeled graphs.
ocar.action: Szalkai, Kerepesi, Varga, and Grolmusz, in Neuroscience Letters (2015; arXiv 2014), present Budapest Reference Connectome Server v2.0, which computes common edges across 96 Human Connectome Project connectomes, each with 1015 Lausanne2008 vertices.
ocar.resolution: Graphs come from HCP S500 DWI of healthy adults aged 22–35, processed with the Connectome Mapper Toolkit, deterministic streamlines, and edge weights n/L (fiber count over mean length). Users set filters; outputs are csv/GraphML with FreeSurfer anatomical labels and a 3D WebGL view. The site is http://connectome.pitgroup.org. Version 1.0 had used six earlier CMTK graphs.
ocar.future_work: The consensus graphs are offered as reduced-error references; how they compare to later HCP releases is outside this extract.

summaries.beginner: No two human brain maps are identical, but many cables show up again and again. This web server lets you download a consensus wiring diagram built from 96 MRI scans, with sliders for how common an edge must be.
summaries.intermediate: Szalkai, Kerepesi, Varga, and Grolmusz (Neuroscience Letters, 2015) describe Budapest Reference Connectome Server v2.0. It identifies common edges among 96 HCP S500 cortical connectomes (1015 ROIs, ~1.5 mm² Lausanne2008 parcels), using Connectome Mapper deterministic tractography. Edge weight is n/L. Median/mean consensus tables drive a website (http://connectome.pitgroup.org) with csv/GraphML download and a modified WebGL Brain Viewer. Version 1.0 used six previously published graphs.
summaries.advanced: Catalog year is 2014; the journal version is 2015. This is a resource paper, not a new biological finding. Deterministic streamline graphs inherit known tracking biases. Age range 22–35 and October 2014 download date are those stated. No independent error rate versus tracers is in the extract.

plain_language_summary: No two human brain maps are identical, but many cables show up again and again. This web server lets you download a consensus wiring diagram built from 96 MRI scans, with sliders for how common an edge must be.

ocar.opportunity: Layer 6 in visual cortex sends both cortico-cortical and cortico-thalamic signals; knowing each cell class’s stimulus tuning and who synapses onto it would explain how context and feature information are routed.
ocar.challenge: L6 principal cells are diverse, and bulk recordings cannot assign sensory selectivity or long-range inputs to identified CC versus CT projection neurons.
ocar.action: Vélez-Fort, Rousseau, Niedworok, Wickersham, Rancz, Brown, Strom, and Margrie, in Neuron (2014), combine whole-cell recording from identified L6 cells in anesthetized adult C57BL/6 mouse V1 with modified rabies monosynaptic input mapping.
ocar.resolution: CC-projecting cells span a broad orientation-selectivity spectrum and are innervated mainly by deep-layer V1 neurons. CT-projecting cells are ultrasparse-firing, sharply tuned for orientation and direction, and receive long-range input from higher cortical areas. The authors interpret this as segregated microcircuits for contextual versus stimulus-specific feedback, including possible stimulus-specific thalamic gain control.
ocar.future_work: Presynaptic functional identity was not recorded, so intra- versus interlaminar contributions to subthreshold tuning remain to be established, as do possible CC subclasses.

summaries.beginner: Deep in mouse visual cortex, two kinds of output cells do different jobs. One talks mostly to other cortical cells and is loosely tuned; the other talks to thalamus, fires very rarely, and is extremely picky about orientation and direction.
summaries.intermediate: Vélez-Fort et al. (Neuron, 2014) record identified layer-6 principal cells in mouse V1 and map monosynaptic inputs with modified rabies. Cortico-cortical cells show a broad range of orientation selectivity and predominantly local deep-layer innervation. Cortico-thalamic cells fire extremely sparsely, are exquisitely orientation- and direction-tuned, and receive long-range higher-area input. Discussion links CT axons to dLGN and TRN as a possible stimulus-specific thalamic gain-control signal, and to modulation of layers 5–6 and upper layers via polysynaptic routes.
summaries.advanced: Animals are anesthetized 5–8-week C57BL/6 mice (fentanyl/midazolam/medetomidine). ‘Ultrasparse’ is qualitative in the extract. Functional identity of rabies-labeled presynaptic cells is not measured. Open-access Neuron PDF (© 2014 The Authors).

plain_language_summary: Deep in mouse visual cortex, two kinds of output cells do different jobs. One talks mostly to other cortical cells and is loosely tuned; the other talks to thalamus, fires very rarely, and is extremely picky about orientation and direction.

ocar.opportunity: The retina is the first stage of vision and a proving ground for whether parallel channels are exclusive microcircuits or unique combinations of shared parts.
ocar.challenge: Convergence and divergence even in retina undermine a simple dedicated-pathway model, and any one method (EM, physiology, or light microscopy) can mislead about wiring.
ocar.action: Dunn and Wong, in Journal of Physiology (2014), review mouse retinal wiring, diagramming current knowledge and open puzzles and urging multi-method verification.
ocar.resolution: They argue that parallel channels more likely emerge from unique combinations of microcircuits than from exclusive pathways, and they collect structural and functional evidence across serial EM, electrophysiology, and light microscopy for the mouse retina.
ocar.future_work: The review’s stated need is to test proposed connectivity with more than one method so that circuits are verified both structurally and functionally.

summaries.beginner: The eye’s retina was thought to send visual features down separate private cables. This review of the mouse retina says the channels share parts, and that electron microscopy, physiology, and light microscopy must be combined before we trust a wiring diagram.
summaries.intermediate: Dunn and Wong (Journal of Physiology, 2014) write a topical review of mouse retinal wiring. They contrast a classic parallel-processor view with accumulating convergence and divergence even at the first visual stage, and they argue that channels arise from combinatorial microcircuits. The piece diagrams remaining puzzles and stresses serial EM, electrophysiology, and light microscopy as complementary. Transgenic-mouse tools are noted as a reason the mouse retina is now a standard system.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not a new volume. Catalog method tag is electron microscopy; the paper is explicitly multi-modal. Functional claims in the diagrams should be checked against the cited primary papers. Acknowledgements list a large community of retina colleagues who commented on the manuscript.

plain_language_summary: The eye’s retina was thought to send visual features down separate private cables. This review of the mouse retina says the channels share parts, and that electron microscopy, physiology, and light microscopy must be combined before we trust a wiring diagram.

ocar.opportunity: The word connectome is new, but maps of neural connections are old. Placing modern imaging in that history clarifies what is actually novel.
ocar.challenge: Contemporary definitions still rest on neuron theory from more than a century ago, and many current maps may be inaccurate surrogates of true anatomy.
ocar.action: Catani, Thiebaut de Schotten, Slater, and Dell’Acqua, in NeuroImage (2013), as described in the catalog abstract, trace anatomical and physiological ideas behind modern connectome definitions.
ocar.resolution: The abstract argues that today’s advantage is quantitative imaging that can correlate structure, function, and behaviour, while still warning that a comprehensive human-brain connectome remains far off and that many maps are anatomically unfaithful.
ocar.future_work: How later large-scale projects changed that historical verdict is outside the abstract.

summaries.beginner: People have been drawing maps of brain connections for centuries. This history essay says modern imaging is powerful, but a true complete map of the human brain is still a long way off, and many of today’s pictures are only rough stand-ins.
summaries.intermediate: Catani, Thiebaut de Schotten, Slater, and Dell’Acqua (NeuroImage, 2013) review ‘proto-connectome’ maps and the conceptual origins of the modern term. Per the catalog abstract, they credit current methods with quantitative, multi-modal connectivity measures, while arguing that many contemporary maps remain inaccurate anatomical surrogates and that a comprehensive human connectome is historically distant. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Colpo et al., Scientific Reports (2025), on structural–functional fingerprinting in 41 newly diagnosed glioma patients, not the Catani et al. historical NeuroImage essay. Claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of the 2013 paper is required for the historical argument.

plain_language_summary: People have been drawing maps of brain connections for centuries. This history essay says modern imaging is powerful, but a true complete map of the human brain is still a long way off, and many of today’s pictures are only rough stand-ins.

ocar.opportunity: Birds can match some ape-level cognitive feats despite a nucleated, non-laminar telencephalon. A large-scale wiring diagram would test whether avian and mammalian brains share organizational principles after ~300 million years of separate evolution.
ocar.challenge: Macro-scale connectivity matrices existed for humans and macaques but not for a bird, so graph comparisons were unavailable.
ocar.action: Shanahan, Bingman, Shimizu, Wild, and Güntürkün, in Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience (2013), assemble the first large-scale pigeon forebrain connectivity matrix and analyze it with graph theory.
ocar.resolution: The pigeon telencephalon is reported as a modular small-world network with a connective core of hubs that includes prefrontal-like and hippocampal structures, plus disassortativity and characteristic motifs. Top-level modules are described as functionally analogous to human ones but more anatomically distributed. Hub membership is supported by betweenness, degree, k-core, rich-club, and knotty-centrality analyses.
ocar.future_work: Implications of disassortativity for robustness are flagged as unresolved; the matrix is a literature-collated wiring diagram, not a new tracer census.

summaries.beginner: Bird brains look different from ours—they are built of clumps, not layers—yet some birds are strikingly smart. A wiring diagram of the pigeon forebrain is reported to follow the same high-level network rules as mammal brains: modules, short paths, and a core of hub regions.
summaries.intermediate: Shanahan et al. (Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience, 2013) present a large-scale pigeon telencephalon connectivity matrix and graph analysis. They report high small-world index, modularity (two levels), disassortativity, motif structure, and a connective core of hubs including prefrontal-like and hippocampal regions. Unlike human top-level modules, pigeon modules are more anatomically distributed. The authors interpret this as shared organizational principles despite nucleated versus laminar pallia and deep divergence.
summaries.advanced: This is a collated connectivity matrix plus topology, not an EM or MRI connectome of one pigeon. Table values in the extract (betweenness, participation) are region-wise scores, not a single summary statistic. ‘Functionally analogous’ to human modules is an interpretation. Catalog organism tags are empty; the species is pigeon.

plain_language_summary: Bird brains look different from ours—they are built of clumps, not layers—yet some birds are strikingly smart. A wiring diagram of the pigeon forebrain is reported to follow the same high-level network rules as mammal brains: modules, short paths, and a core of hub regions.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-brain light microscopy is about a terabyte for a mouse, and 1 mm³ of EM is about half a petabyte. Those sizes finally make digital reconstruction of neurons and circuits a computational field.
ocar.challenge: Published large-scale EM analysis had been almost entirely manual (~10^4 work hours), and no single algorithm would solve data management, segmentation, 3D reconstruction, geometry, and mixed human–machine workflows.
ocar.action: Helmstaedter and Mitra, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2012), review computational methods and challenges for large-scale circuit mapping, with emphasis on reconstructing neurons from EM cubes.
ocar.resolution: They frame computational neuroanatomy as a new field aiming at single-neuron morphology and entire circuits. The outlook is gradual performance gains and optimized machine–human annotation rather than one algorithmic breakthrough.
ocar.future_work: Automated analysis still needed advances to cut manual labor substantially; hybrid annotation is expected to dominate in the near term (as of 2012).

summaries.beginner: Photographing even a small piece of brain at synapse scale creates enormous computer files. This 2012 review explains why tracing those pictures still needed people as well as algorithms, and what the software problems were.
summaries.intermediate: Helmstaedter and Mitra (Current Opinion in Neurobiology, 2012) review computational circuit mapping. They size a light-microscopic mouse brain at about a terabyte and 1 mm³ of EM at about half a petabyte, and they list tasks: data management, segmentation, 3D reconstruction, computational geometry, and hybrid manual/algorithmic workflows. Almost all then-published large-scale EM analysis is described as manual, perhaps ~10^4 work hours. The outlook is incremental tool improvement and machine–human interaction, not a single breakthrough.
summaries.advanced: This is a 2012 opinion/review; numbers are order-of-magnitude engineering estimates. The PDF is an NIH Public Access author manuscript (PMC final 2012 July 27). Primary reconstruction results live in the cited papers. Catalog organism is mouse; the review is methods-general.

plain_language_summary: Photographing even a small piece of brain at synapse scale creates enormous computer files. This 2012 review explains why tracing those pictures still needed people as well as algorithms, and what the software problems were.

ocar.opportunity: As high-throughput connectomes arrive, newcomers need a map of which graph and spatial statistics are meaningful at regional and neuronal scales.
ocar.challenge: Metrics at node, module, and whole-network scales are easy to misapply, and spatial wiring-length constraints are often ignored when only topology is reported.
ocar.action: Kaiser, in NeuroImage (2011), writes a tutorial on topological and spatial connectome analysis from microscopic neuron graphs to macroscopic region graphs.
ocar.resolution: The tutorial covers local, regional, and global features; archetypes (Erdős–Rényi, scale-free, small-world, modular, hierarchical); comparison uses such as patients versus controls; and methods for analyzing wiring lengths. Benefits and limitations of each approach are discussed.
ocar.future_work: The piece is pedagogical; the selected extract’s latter portion is references, so individual worked examples should be read in the main text and cited tools (e.g. FANMOD).

summaries.beginner: Once you have a map of brain connections, you still need to know how to score it. This tutorial walks through common network measurements, from single nodes up to the whole graph, and reminds readers that real brains also have a physical length cost.
summaries.intermediate: Kaiser (NeuroImage, 2011) offers an introductory tutorial on connectome analysis at macroscopic (region) and microscopic (neuron) scales. Topics include node-, set-, and network-level topology; random, scale-free, small-world, modular, and hierarchical archetypes; clinical comparison of networks; and spatial wiring-length analysis. The stated audience is new researchers, with explicit discussion of benefits and limits of each measure.
summaries.advanced: This is a tutorial/review, not a new dataset. The selected PDF text is poorly OCR’d at the front (‘running title: Principles of Connectome Analysis’) and ends in the reference list, so later tutorial sections are not in the extract. Treat textbook graph definitions as standard, not Kaiser-original.

plain_language_summary: Once you have a map of brain connections, you still need to know how to score it. This tutorial walks through common network measurements, from single nodes up to the whole graph, and reminds readers that real brains also have a physical length cost.

ocar.opportunity: A directional, genetically targetable transsynaptic tracer would let experimenters map who talks to whom in the intact mammalian CNS, not only who sits nearby.
ocar.challenge: Existing viral tracers did not give a single platform that could be switched between anterograde and retrograde transsynaptic spread, or restricted to monosynaptic jumps from defined starter cells.
ocar.action: Beier, Saunders, Oldenburg, Miyamichi, Akhtar, Luo, Whelan, Sabatini, and Cepko, in PNAS (2011), engineer vesicular stomatitis virus vectors with glycoproteins from other viruses and test them in mouse brain, slices, and electrophysiology.
ocar.resolution: Lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus G produced specifically anterograde transsynaptic spread; rabies G produced specifically retrograde spread. An avian G fusion allowed targeting of cells that express an avian receptor, enabling monosynaptic anterograde tracing from defined cells. Slice recordings confirmed synaptic connectivity of labeled pairs. In vivo infections matched predicted anterograde or retrograde patterns.
ocar.future_work: Cytotoxicity and host shut-off of VSV remain practical limits noted in the related-work citations; broader circuit applications are implied rather than exhaustively mapped here.

summaries.beginner: To draw a circuit diagram you need a way to see which cells actually talk to which. This team retunes a livestock virus so it hops synapses forward, backward, or just one step from a chosen starting cell in the mouse brain.
summaries.intermediate: Beier et al. (PNAS, 2011) use vesicular stomatitis virus with swapped glycoproteins as CNS tracers. LCMV G yields anterograde transsynaptic labeling; rabies G yields retrograde labeling. An avian G fusion restricts infection to cells expressing an avian receptor, demonstrating monosynaptic anterograde tracing from defined starters. Electrophysiology in slice cultures is used to show synaptic connectivity between labeled pairs. Mouse in vivo infections produced the expected directional patterns.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods/resource paper. Directionality is G-protein-dependent viral spread, not EM-verified synapses in every area tested. Cytotoxicity of VSV is a known issue in the cited virology. The extract’s end is references. Catalog stage tag ‘proofreading’ is not the paper’s topic.

plain_language_summary: To draw a circuit diagram you need a way to see which cells actually talk to which. This team retunes a livestock virus so it hops synapses forward, backward, or just one step from a chosen starting cell in the mouse brain.

ocar.opportunity: Behavior is computed by neurons plus a biochemical neuromodulator network that dynamically rewrites the wiring diagram. Understanding that overlay would explain why a static synapse list is not enough.
ocar.challenge: Modulator actions can be combinatorially complex, so experiments and theory that treat the connectome as a fixed graph miss the computation.
ocar.action: Brezina, in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (2010), reviews how neuromodulator networks operate, using examples including Aplysia neuromuscular modulation, and asks how their structural and functional ‘logic’ might be reverse-engineered.
ocar.resolution: The review treats modulators as a second computational network that combines with the neuronal network. It discusses experimental and conceptual problems this poses and points to systems-biology and engineering methods (including global-structure analyses and reverse-engineering) as possible routes to understanding.
ocar.future_work: Granting modulators an independent computational role, and mapping that role onto identified circuits, is presented as the outstanding program rather than a completed result.

summaries.beginner: A list of synapses is not a complete recipe for behavior, because chemical modulators constantly retune those synapses. This essay explains that extra chemical network and why it makes brains harder to read from wiring alone.
summaries.intermediate: Brezina (Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B, 2010) reviews neuromodulator networks as a biochemical overlay on the neuronal wiring diagram. Using work including Aplysia neuromuscular junction modulation, he argues that the synapse map alone cannot specify the computation underlying behavior. The article discusses experimental difficulties and suggests analyzing the structural/functional logic of modulatory networks, including engineering reverse-engineering approaches.
summaries.advanced: This is a review/perspective, not a connectomic reconstruction. Aplysia examples are from the author’s prior work (cited). The selected extract moves from a model-figure discussion into references. NIH grant NS41497 funded the author’s described work.

plain_language_summary: A list of synapses is not a complete recipe for behavior, because chemical modulators constantly retune those synapses. This essay explains that extra chemical network and why it makes brains harder to read from wiring alone.

ocar.opportunity: A high-fidelity whole-human-brain computational model would need organ-scale ultrastructure preserved after death, with agonal and postmortem damage minimized. Physician-assisted death could in principle provide a short, controlled interval before perfusion.
ocar.challenge: Standard postmortem delays destroy connectomic ultrastructure, and existing aldehyde-stabilized cryopreservation had to be made compatible with a human PAD-like timeline and large-mammal vasculature.
ocar.action: Song, LaVergne, and Wróbel, on bioRxiv (2026), adapt aldehyde-stabilized cryopreservation for pigs as a cardiovascular and brain-size model, then assess preservation with light microscopy and volume EM (wafer-SEM and FIB-SEM).
ocar.resolution: They report connectomically traceable whole pig brains and propose storage around −35 °C expected to keep ultrastructure and macromolecules stable for thousands of years. They identify about 14 minutes after cardiac arrest as the approximate perfusability window in which blood washout must start.
ocar.future_work: Human PAD application is proposed, not demonstrated. Authors are Nectome employees offering commercial preservation.

summaries.beginner: To keep a whole large brain looking intact under an electron microscope after death, blood has to be washed out very quickly. In pigs, this team reports a preservation protocol meant to match a human medically assisted death, with a roughly 14-minute window after the heart stops.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (7 March 2026), Song, LaVergne, and Wróbel modify aldehyde-stabilized cryopreservation for whole pig brains as a stand-in for human physician-assisted death. Light microscopy plus wafer-SEM and FIB-SEM (Hayworth/Janelia) are used to argue that the brains are connectomically traceable. They state that washout must begin within about 14 min of cardiac arrest, and they propose −35 °C storage without ultrastructural degradation for thousands of years. IACUC: BioDevelopment Associates 220601MP.
summaries.advanced: This is a company preprint (Nectome Inc.); all three authors are employees of a for-profit preservation firm—a first-order conflict of interest. ‘Thousands of years’ and ‘connectomically traceable’ are authorship claims. The 14 min figure is an approximate perfusability window in pigs, not a human trial. Volume EM of samples is not a whole-brain connectome.

plain_language_summary: To keep a whole large brain looking intact under an electron microscope after death, blood has to be washed out very quickly. In pigs, this team reports a preservation protocol meant to match a human medically assisted death, with a roughly 14-minute window after the heart stops.

ocar.opportunity: Mesoscopic mouse connectomes plus cell-class maps make it possible to ask which areas can hold working memory without sensory input, and whether coding is local or distributed.
ocar.challenge: Available connectomic data lack the cell-type-specific long-range targeting needed to explain neural dynamics; it was also unclear whether delay activity is generated locally or by multi-area reverberation.
ocar.action: Ding, Froudist-Walsh, Jaramillo, Jiang, and Wang, in eLife (2024), build a large-scale mouse-brain working-memory model on interareal cortical connections plus a macroscopic gradient of parvalbumin interneuron density.
ocar.resolution: Mnemonic coding is distributed yet modular; spatial patterns depend on long-range cell-type-specific targeting and class densities. Cell-type-specific graph measures predict activity patterns and a core subnetwork for memory maintenance. The model has numerous attractor states, each engaging a distinct subset of areas. Cortical and thalamocortical recurrent loops help sustain delay activity.
ocar.future_work: The authors emphasize that connectome databases must be supplemented with cell-type-specific information, and they offer experimental predictions that distinguish local versus long-distance generation of persistent firing.

summaries.beginner: Working memory is the brain’s scratchpad. A computer model of the mouse brain that includes which cell types project where predicts that memory traces live across many regions, not in one spot, and that inhibitory cell density helps set the pattern.
summaries.intermediate: Ding, Froudist-Walsh, Jaramillo, Jiang, and Xiao-Jing Wang (eLife, 2024) construct a multi-regional mouse working-memory model from mesoscopic cortical connectome data and a measured PV-interneuron density gradient. They report distributed yet modular mnemonic coding, prediction of activity patterns from cell-type-specific graph measures, a core subnetwork for maintenance, and many attractor states (distinct area subsets). Recurrent cortico-cortical and thalamocortical loops aid delay activity. The discussion stresses that cell-type-specific connectomics is required to explain distributed cognition.
summaries.advanced: This is a large-scale dynamical model, not new anatomy. Persistent-firing locality versus long-range reverberation is posed as an experimental test, not settled. PDF is the eLife research article (eLife 2024;12:e85442). ‘Numerous attractor states’ should be read as model phenomenology.

plain_language_summary: Working memory is the brain’s scratchpad. A computer model of the mouse brain that includes which cell types project where predicts that memory traces live across many regions, not in one spot, and that inhibitory cell density helps set the pattern.

ocar.opportunity: Coordinated multi-body-part actions such as grooming are a tractable place to ask how a nervous system synchronizes effectors, using a complete fly brain connectome.
ocar.challenge: It was unknown whether coordination requires proprioceptive coupling among head, antennae, and forelegs, or whether a central controller can co-recruit motor networks.
ocar.action: Özdil, Arreguit, Scherrer, Ijspeert, and Ramdya, on bioRxiv (2024), combine Drosophila antennal-grooming kinematics, a biomechanical simulation, lesion/immobilization experiments, and a grooming network built from the fly brain connectome, plus a simulated activation screen.
ocar.resolution: Unilateral or bilateral antennal grooming arises from synchronized head, antenna, and foreleg movements that a biomechanical replay shows make tibia–antenna collisions more efficient. Amputation or head immobilization does not stop the other parts, implying coordination is not required proprioceptive feedback. Central interneurons and shared premotor neurons link neck, antennal, and foreleg motor networks. Two motifs—recurrent excitation promoting contralateral antennal pitch and broadcast inhibition suppressing ipsilateral pitch—account for unilateral coordination in the screen.
ocar.future_work: The authors suggest similarly centralized controllers may co-recruit body parts for other behaviors; those generalizations are not demonstrated here.

summaries.beginner: When a fly grooms its antennae, the head, antennae, and front legs move together on purpose. Mapping the responsible neurons in the fly connectome points to a central controller, not a chain of reflexes that wait on each body part to feel the others.
summaries.intermediate: Özdil et al. (bioRxiv, 17 December 2024) study goal-directed antennal grooming in Drosophila. Kinematics plus a biomechanical model indicate that coordination yields unobstructed, forceful tibia–antenna collisions. Foreleg or antenna amputation, or head immobilization, leaves other parts moving, so proprioceptive coupling is not required. A connectome-derived antennal-grooming network implicates centralized interneurons and shared premotor neurons. A simulated activation screen highlights a recurrent excitatory motif for contralateral antennal pitch and broadcast inhibition of ipsilateral pitch.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint. The extract’s later pages are references; quantitative screen results live in figures not fully captured. ‘Comprehensive’ network means a reconstructed subgraph from the fly brain connectome, not a new EM volume. Catalog method tags are empty; the work is connectome analysis plus behavior and modeling.

plain_language_summary: When a fly grooms its antennae, the head, antennae, and front legs move together on purpose. Mapping the responsible neurons in the fly connectome points to a central controller, not a chain of reflexes that wait on each body part to feel the others.

ocar.opportunity: Neurons must choose synaptic partners and also avoid unwanted neighbors. A combinatorial cell-surface code could implement that avoidance in neocortex.
ocar.challenge: How clustered protocadherin gamma (γ-PCDH) isoform combinations map onto actual cortical synaptic probability was unclear, including whether effects are limited to lineage-related cells.
ocar.action: Zhu, Deng, Fan, Wang, Zhou, and Xu, in eLife (2024), combine 5′ end single-cell sequencing of γ-PCDH variable isoforms with whole-cell pair recordings in mouse neocortex, plus knockout and overexpression manipulations.
ocar.resolution: Neocortical neurons express intricate combinatorial γ-PCDH isoform patterns. As combinatorial similarity between neurons increased, synaptic connectivity decreased. Connection rate rose between adjacent pyramids in pcdhg knockouts and fell when neurons overexpressed single or multiple identical variable isoforms, including between non-lineage cells. The authors treat this as a repulsion mechanism for synapse formation.
ocar.future_work: Subtle differences versus prior studies (Molumby et al., Tarusawa et al.) are noted; how the code scales to full cortical connectomes remains open.

summaries.beginner: Brain cells need a way to avoid wiring to the wrong neighbors. In mouse cortex, cells that wear more similar combinations of γ-protocadherin surface proteins are less likely to synapse, like a molecular ‘do not connect if we match’ rule.
summaries.intermediate: Zhu et al. (eLife, 2024) profile combinatorial γ-PCDH variable-isoform expression in mouse neocortical neurons with 5′ end single-cell sequencing and test connectivity with whole-cell patch clamp. Higher isoform-pattern similarity predicts lower connection probability. pcdhg knockout increases synaptic connection rate between adjacent pyramids; overexpressing identical isoforms decreases it, not only among lineage-related cells. Sequential in utero electroporation (E14.5/E15.5) is used to control isoform overlap. The finding is framed as repulsion supporting network construction.
summaries.advanced: The supplied extract includes an eLife versioned preprint header (eLife.89532.1 / 2023) of the 2024 paper. Similarity-level experiments are in Figure 4; exact percentages are not in the selected text. Catalog title says ‘synaptic connectivity’; the PDF title uses ‘synaptic specificity’—same study. This is physiology plus sequencing, not EM.

plain_language_summary: Brain cells need a way to avoid wiring to the wrong neighbors. In mouse cortex, cells that wear more similar combinations of γ-protocadherin surface proteins are less likely to synapse, like a molecular ‘do not connect if we match’ rule.

ocar.opportunity: Demand for TEM and especially volume EM is rising while trained staff retire. Faster, less hands-on specimen preparation would free laboratories.
ocar.challenge: Manual TEM prep typically takes 1–3 days and vEM 3–5 days of frequent reagent exchanges, using skilled labor and toxic chemicals.
ocar.action: Goodman, Benson, Flint, Dye, Chimento, Phillips, Percival, and Kidd, in Microscopy Today (2024), present four case studies of mPrep Automated Specimen Processors (ASP-1000 and ASP-2000) in academic, preclinical, and clinical labs.
ocar.resolution: They report TEM-style infiltration prior to resin curing in 1–4 hours and vEM preparation in 6–8 hours, with quality compared to manual processing in cited work and a nerve case study. ASPs can run many specimens at once (examples: up to 128 tissue pieces, 16 samples, 24 nerves, or 32 vEM specimens with 4 pieces per capsule) using 4–5 ml per reagent step.
ocar.future_work: The article is a vendor-inclusive workflow report; independent multi-lab trials of connectomic-grade ultrastructure are not the dataset here.

summaries.beginner: Getting tissue ready for electron microscopy usually takes days of timed chemical baths. This lab-practice article describes machines that automate those baths, cutting the wait and the hands-on time for ordinary TEM and for 3D volume EM.
summaries.intermediate: Goodman et al. (Microscopy Today, January 2024) describe mPrep Automated Specimen Processors in four case studies. They contrast typical manual TEM (1–3 days) and vEM (≥4 days) with ASP times of 1–4 hours (TEM-style) and 6–8 hours (vEM), comparable in speed to microwave processing but with less hands-on effort and reagent use. Batch examples include up to 128 tissue pieces or 32 vEM specimens. Protocols can include immunolabeling and other complex steps.
summaries.advanced: This is a Microscopy Today methods/workflow piece involving Microscopy Innovations hardware (mPrep ASP). Times and batch sizes are manufacturer-and-user case studies, not a randomized quality trial. The PDF bears a Johns Hopkins download stamp (26 August 2026). Connectomic image quality must be judged from the cited case studies, not assumed.

plain_language_summary: Getting tissue ready for electron microscopy usually takes days of timed chemical baths. This lab-practice article describes machines that automate those baths, cutting the wait and the hands-on time for ordinary TEM and for 3D volume EM.

ocar.opportunity: Principles of cortical microcircuit connectivity have been inferred mostly from rodents. Direct human layer 2–3 measurements would show whether those rules transfer to an evolutionarily expanded cortex.
ocar.challenge: It was unclear whether human temporal-cortex pyramids show rodent-like reciprocity, strength–probability coupling, and cyclic motifs.
ocar.action: Peng and colleagues, in Science (2024), as described in the catalog abstract, analyze multineuron patch-clamp recordings from layer 2–3 pyramidal neurons in human temporal cortex obtained during surgery, and compare network properties with rodents.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports that human connectivity is heterogeneous, reciprocity is random, synaptic strength is independent of connection probability, and the graph is directed and mostly acyclic. Putting those principles into neural-network models increased dimensionality and improved performance on functionally relevant tasks.
ocar.future_work: How widely the directed-acyclic motif holds outside supragranular temporal cortex is outside the abstract.

summaries.beginner: Most of what we know about how cortical cells wire to their neighbors comes from rodents. Recordings from human surgical tissue suggest a different pattern: connections run mostly one way, with few loops, which models say may help the network compute in higher dimensions.
summaries.intermediate: Peng et al. (Science, 2024) study human layer 2–3 temporal-cortex microcircuits with multi-neuron patch clamp on surgical samples. Per the catalog abstract (and editor’s summary), unlike rodents, connectivity is heterogeneous, reciprocity is random, strength does not follow connection probability, and topology is directed and mostly acyclic. Implementing those rules in models increased dimensionality and task performance. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Reimann, Egas Santander, Kanari, and Barros-Zulaica, iScience (2026), on spatial continuity of neurons explaining non-random network architecture, not the Peng et al. human L2/3 Science paper. Claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of Science eadg8828 is required for sample size, statistics, and rodent comparison details.

plain_language_summary: Most of what we know about how cortical cells wire to their neighbors comes from rodents. Recordings from human surgical tissue suggest a different pattern: connections run mostly one way, with few loops, which models say may help the network compute in higher dimensions.

ocar.opportunity: Negative valence bias is central to depression, yet the amygdala circuits that could assign too much aversiveness to cues are hard to isolate in humans. A mouse model with a matching olfactory bias would let those circuits be traced.
ocar.challenge: Limits of human imaging resolution impede easy amygdala segmentation into valence-specific pathways, so circuit-level tests require rodents plus a clinically parallel bias.
ocar.action: Bigot and colleagues, in Translational Psychiatry (2024), study chronic corticosterone (CORT) mice, compare odor-value assignment with bipolar depressed patients, and use CTB and rabies tracing plus ex vivo activity and chemogenetics on BLA projection classes.
ocar.resolution: CORT mice show an antidepressant-responsive negative bias in olfactory valence, paralleling patient odor-value changes. BLA-to-NAc neurons (preferentially positive valence) are less recruited and BLA-to-CeA neurons (preferentially negative valence) more recruited. Chemogenetic hyperactivation of BLA-to-NAc neurons dampens the dysfunction. Altered BLA activity correlates with durable presynaptic changes from paraventricular thalamus.
ocar.future_work: The authors present these BLA circuits as a translational target for understanding treatment; human causal tests are not performed.

summaries.beginner: Depression often makes the world look more threatening. In mice given a stress hormone, and in people with bipolar depression, smells are valued more negatively, and the study traces that shift to a split in amygdala output paths—one toward reward circuits, one toward fear circuits.
summaries.intermediate: Bigot et al. (Translational Psychiatry, 2024) report that chronic CORT mice assign more negative valence to odors, a bias that responds to antidepressant treatment and parallels odor-value changes in bipolar depressed patients. Tracing and activity measurements show decreased recruitment of BLA neurons projecting to nucleus accumbens and increased recruitment of BLA neurons projecting to central amygdala. Chemogenetic activation of BLA-to-NAc cells reduced the dysfunction. Presynaptic remodeling from paraventricular thalamus is correlated with the altered BLA activity.
summaries.advanced: This is a mouse CORT model plus a patient odor-assignment parallel, not a human circuit-causal study. ‘Supports’ in the title is the authors’ causal framing; chemogenetics tests one projection class. Catalog stages include segmentation/proofreading, which do not describe the paper. CC BY-NC-ND license; Translational Psychiatry (2024) 14:382.

plain_language_summary: Depression often makes the world look more threatening. In mice given a stress hormone, and in people with bipolar depression, smells are valued more negatively, and the study traces that shift to a split in amygdala output paths—one toward reward circuits, one toward fear circuits.

ocar.opportunity: Memory models often store items as excitatory assemblies. If assemblies also contain matched inhibition (E/I assemblies), representations might stay balanced and geometrically organized rather than collapsing into discrete attractors.
ocar.challenge: Classic attractor memory networks and purely excitatory assemblies with global inhibition make different predictions; biologically realistic spiking constraints from a piriform-like cortex were needed to tell them apart.
ocar.action: Meissner-Bernard, Zenke, and Friedrich, as an eLife reviewed preprint (2024; DOI 10.7554/eLife.96303), build a spiking network from data on adult zebrafish area Dp (piriform homolog), a precisely balanced recurrent network, and compare E/I assemblies with excitatory assemblies plus global inhibition.
ocar.resolution: E/I assemblies stabilize firing-rate distributions. The network does not show discrete attractor dynamics; learned-input responses are constrained onto manifolds that focus activity into subspaces. Covariance structure supports pattern classification from selected subsets. Geometry is intermediate between geometry-preserving random networks and discrete maps, becoming more map-like if assembly amplification rises or synaptic-balance precision falls.
ocar.future_work: The authors suggest such continuous representations could support continual and higher-order learning; those capabilities are discussed, not fully benchmarked as a cognitive suite.

summaries.beginner: Memory is often imagined as a set of on/off basins in a network. A model based on a fish brain area like olfactory cortex instead keeps excitation and inhibition co-tuned, so memories look like smooth shapes in activity space rather than a few rigid attractors.
summaries.intermediate: Meissner-Bernard, Zenke, and Friedrich (eLife reviewed preprint, 2024) simulate a spiking network constrained by zebrafish Dp, homologous to piriform cortex. E/I assemblies (co-tuned excitation and inhibition) stabilize rate distributions relative to excitatory assemblies with global inhibition and do not produce discrete attractors. Learned inputs lie on manifolds whose covariance supports classification from chosen neuronal subsets. Tuned networks sit between geometry-preserving transforms and discrete maps; more within-assembly amplification or less precise balance pushes them toward map-like behavior.
summaries.advanced: Catalog journal field is bioRxiv; the extract is an eLife reviewed preprint (v2). This is a data-constrained model of Dp, not a new EM connectome. Geometric claims are simulation outcomes. Organism tag is zebrafish; ‘related to olfactory cortex’ is homology, not a mammalian experiment.

plain_language_summary: Memory is often imagined as a set of on/off basins in a network. A model based on a fish brain area like olfactory cortex instead keeps excitation and inhibition co-tuned, so memories look like smooth shapes in activity space rather than a few rigid attractors.

ocar.opportunity: Animals continuously choose the next action in the real world, but lab decision neuroscience has mostly used artificial trials. Genetic tools and connectomes now make naturalistic choice experimentally tractable in small nervous systems.
ocar.challenge: Trial-structured tasks may miss the neural logic of ongoing, innate decisions such as defensive choices.
ocar.action: Asinof and Card, in Annual Review of Neuroscience (2024), as described in the catalog abstract, propose ‘reverse neuroethology’: pick experimentally accessible animals and use connectomes and genetic reagents to follow information flow during naturalistic choice, illustrated with Drosophila defensive behaviors.
ocar.resolution: The abstract presents this strategy as a way to study innate, rapid decision making, focusing on defensive behavioral choices in Drosophila melanogaster.
ocar.future_work: How far the framework extends beyond fly defense is left as a program for the field.

summaries.beginner: Lab studies of decisions often use unnatural trials, while real animals keep choosing what to do next in a messy world. This review proposes studying those natural choices in genetically tractable animals such as flies, using connectomes as a map.
summaries.intermediate: Asinof and Card (Annual Review of Neuroscience, 2024) propose reverse neuroethology: choose animal models for experimental access, then use connectomes and genetically encoded tools to analyze information flow during naturalistic choices. Per the catalog abstract, they focus on innate, rapid decisions, especially defensive behaviors in Drosophila melanogaster. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Wang, Yang, Liu, Gao, Lv, Zhang, Ning, and Sun, Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience (2026), on convergence–divergence circuits for multimodal integration of innate and learned opponent valences, not the Asinof and Card Annual Review. Claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of the 2024 review is required.

plain_language_summary: Lab studies of decisions often use unnatural trials, while real animals keep choosing what to do next in a messy world. This review proposes studying those natural choices in genetically tractable animals such as flies, using connectomes as a map.

ocar.opportunity: Osmium tetroxide is the workhorse lipid stain for biological EM, including synapse-resolution brain imaging. Knowing which osmium species actually generates contrast would guide better staining protocols.
ocar.challenge: Osmium speciation in membranes and the physical basis of EM contrast remained open, limiting rational protocol design.
ocar.action: Li, Wildenberg, Boergens, Yang, Weber, Rieger, Arcidiacono, Klie, Kasthuri, and King, in ChemBioChem (2024), as described in the catalog abstract, use photoemission electron microscopy on Os-stained mouse brain to determine nanoscale electronic structure.
ocar.resolution: The abstract identifies Os(IV) as OsO2 nanoaggregates in lipid membranes, with a metallic density of states near the Fermi level that enhances EM signal and specimen conductivity.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents this assignment as an opening for improved high-contrast staining protocols.

summaries.beginner: Brain tissue is stained with osmium so electron microscopes can see membranes. This chemistry paper reports that the dark contrast comes from metallic osmium dioxide specks in the lipids, which also help the sample conduct electrons.
summaries.intermediate: Li et al. (ChemBioChem, 2024) follow PEEM imaging of mouse brain at synaptic resolution by mapping the electronic structure of osmium-stained tissue. Per the catalog abstract, Os(IV) as OsO2 forms nanoaggregates in lipid membranes, creating spatially varying density of states and a metallic electronic structure near the Fermi level that boosts EM contrast and conductivity. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Garrood et al., Free Neuropathology (2025), evaluating ultrastructural preservation quality in banked brain tissue, not the Li et al. OsO2 PEEM chemistry paper. Claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of ChemBioChem 202400311 is required for spectra and staining implications.

plain_language_summary: Brain tissue is stained with osmium so electron microscopes can see membranes. This chemistry paper reports that the dark contrast comes from metallic osmium dioxide specks in the lipids, which also help the sample conduct electrons.

ocar.opportunity: Perineuronal nets (PNNs) encapsulate synapses on many CNS neurons and change in schizophrenia, epilepsy, Alzheimer’s disease, stroke, and trauma. High-resolution microscopy plus AI could relate mesh microstructure to synapses and disease.
ocar.challenge: The functional meaning of PNN microstructure had been understudied, and tracing mesh units around boutons is laborious.
ocar.action: Paveliev and colleagues, in International Journal of Molecular Sciences (2024), review PNN microstructural changes in brain disorders, high-resolution studies of mesh units around synaptic boutons, PNNs as drug targets, and they report a machine-learning-assisted tool for PNN mesh contour tracing.
ocar.resolution: The review links PNN alterations to several pathologies, discusses ECM–synapse mutual regulation at mesh resolution, updates pharmacological targeting, and presents an ML-assisted contour tracer as a first AI-assisted PNN microscopy step matching the multi-scale complexity of PNN biology.
ocar.future_work: Broader AI models that span synapse to whole-brain PNN organization are proposed rather than demonstrated as a finished connectome tool.

summaries.beginner: Many brain cells wear a lattice of sugars and proteins, a perineuronal net, around their synapses. This review explains how that lattice looks under the microscope in disease, and it introduces a machine-learning helper for tracing the lattice’s outlines.
summaries.intermediate: Paveliev et al. (Int. J. Mol. Sci., 2024) review perineuronal-net microscopy from pathology to AI. They cover PNN changes in schizophrenia and other disorders, high-resolution mesh units surrounding boutons, PNNs as pharmacological targets, and the mismatch between PNN biology’s many scales and prior analysis tools. They report a machine-learning-assisted PNN mesh contour tracer. Confocal PNN data acknowledged from Alexander Dityatev; EM method discussion credited to Ilya Belevich.
summaries.advanced: This is a review plus a reported ML tracing tool, not a new disease cohort. The extract’s end is author contributions/funding (PRIORITY-2030). Catalog stage ‘proofreading’ is not the paper’s topic. Treat therapeutic targeting as literature synthesis.

plain_language_summary: Many brain cells wear a lattice of sugars and proteins, a perineuronal net, around their synapses. This review explains how that lattice looks under the microscope in disease, and it introduces a machine-learning helper for tracing the lattice’s outlines.

ocar.opportunity: Hormones from brain neurosecretory cells (NSC) coordinate sleep, feeding, growth, metabolism, and reproduction. A synaptic connectome of those cells would show how sensory and descending systems regulate endocrine output.
ocar.challenge: NSC dendrites sit in the subesophageal zone, yet it was unclear whether peripheral gustatory neurons synapse on them directly, and NSC synaptic outputs looked sparse relative to their physiological reach.
ocar.action: McKim, Gera, Gayban, Christie, Shin, Reinhard, Manoli, Hilpert, Callaerts, van Breugel, Helfrich-Förster, and Zandawala, on bioRxiv (2024; FlyWire v783), reconstruct the synaptic connectome of adult Drosophila pars intercerebralis/pars lateralis NSC classes, with dynamical modeling and functional tests of corazonin NSC and DNg27.
ocar.resolution: Diuretic hormone 44 NSC emerge as a major integrative hub. Gustatory inputs to NSC are largely indirect despite SEZ dendrites; diverse olfactory paths are mapped. Linear dynamical modeling ranks enteric neurons as the strongest influencers of NSC activity among sensory modalities. Descending neurons provide substantial NSC input, suggesting coordinated endocrine and motor output. Synaptic output is sparse and mostly from corazonin NSC; both CRZ NSC and downstream DNg27 influence egg-laying. Paracrine peptide paths are explored via single-cell transcriptomes.
ocar.future_work: The authors offer the map as a platform to disrupt endocrine pathways relevant to diabetes, hypertension, and infertility; those disease links are prospective.

summaries.beginner: Flies, like us, use brain hormones to run the body. This preprint charts who synapses onto the fly’s hormone cells and finds that gut-related neurons are especially influential, while the hormone cells themselves make few conventional synapses—except a corazonin pathway tied to egg-laying.
summaries.intermediate: McKim et al. (bioRxiv, 2024; updated 2026 in the extract header) analyze the FlyWire v783 synaptic connectome of adult Drosophila neurosecretory cells. DH44 NSC are implicated as a major coordinator. Peripheral taste inputs are largely indirect. Olfactory pathways to NSC are deciphered. Dynamical modeling identifies enteric neurons as the strongest sensory-class influencers. Descending neurons synapse heavily onto NSC. Output synapses are sparse and mostly from corazonin cells; CRZ NSC and DNg27 affect egg-laying (Kir2.1 and optogenetic tests in methods). Transcriptomes address putative paracrine peptide routes.
summaries.advanced: This is a bioRxiv preprint using an existing FlyWire snapshot (v783), not a new EM volume. ‘Strongest influencers’ comes from linear dynamical modeling, not in vivo ranking of all senses. Disease language in the outlook is translational framing. The selected extract’s latter portion is methods (strains, immunohistochemistry).

plain_language_summary: Flies, like us, use brain hormones to run the body. This preprint charts who synapses onto the fly’s hormone cells and finds that gut-related neurons are especially influential, while the hormone cells themselves make few conventional synapses—except a corazonin pathway tied to egg-laying.

ocar.opportunity: Cerebellar learning is thought to require long-term depression at granule-cell to Purkinje-cell synapses when climbing-fibre error signals arrive. A circuit that briefly lifts inhibition at those moments would protect LTD.
ocar.challenge: Inhibitory inputs to Purkinje cells can disrupt LTD, so it was unclear how depression proceeds when interneurons are active in the molecular layer.
ocar.action: Park, Gim, Bahn, Kim, Im, Lee, Lee, Kim, Lee, and Kim, on bioRxiv (2023), analyze synaptic connectivity among neurons reconstructed from serial EM of cerebellar molecular layer and test a computational model of a feedforward disinhibitory motif.
ocar.resolution: They report synapses from climbing fibres onto a subset of inhibitory interneurons (IN1) that synapse onto remaining interneurons (IN2) that in turn inhibit Purkinje cells, redefining interneuron types by connectivity. Together with CF-to-PC synapses this is a feedforward disinhibitory circuit argued to suppress inhibition whenever CF input—and thus LTD—should occur. A model is used to validate the hypothesis.
ocar.future_work: The authors generalize to a principle that disinhibition supports synaptic plasticity; in vivo confirmation of the IN1/IN2 split is implied.

summaries.beginner: The cerebellum learns by weakening some synapses when an error signal arrives, but nearby inhibitory cells can block that weakening. An electron-microscope wiring map suggests the error fibres also turn off those inhibitors at the right moment, giving learning a clear shot.
summaries.intermediate: Park et al. (bioRxiv, 15 September 2023) reconstruct cerebellar molecular-layer connectivity from serial EM. Climbing fibres synapse onto a subset of inhibitory interneurons (IN1) that inhibit another subset (IN2) that inhibit Purkinje cells, forming a feedforward disinhibitory loop alongside CF-to-PC synapses. Interneuron types are redefined by this connectivity rather than only morphology or molecules. A computational model is used to argue that the motif secures granule-to-Purkinje LTD when CF input arrives. Extended Data compare IN1/IN2 dendrite density, axon complexity, and synapse distances (Mann–Whitney tests).
summaries.advanced: This is a 2023 preprint; the selected extract is front matter plus extended-data figure captions rather than a full discussion. IN1/IN2 labels are connectivity-based in this volume. Extended Data p-values (e.g. axon complexity p=0.023, N=20 vs 6) are fragment/cell samples, not a whole-cerebellum census. Catalog dimension is neuroai; the paper is EM plus a model.

plain_language_summary: The cerebellum learns by weakening some synapses when an error signal arrives, but nearby inhibitory cells can block that weakening. An electron-microscope wiring map suggests the error fibres also turn off those inhibitors at the right moment, giving learning a clear shot.

ocar.opportunity: Human imaging consistently finds glucose hypometabolism in aging and neurodegenerative disease, especially in densely interconnected long-range hubs of the connectome. Understanding axonal bioenergetics could explain early axonopathy.
ocar.challenge: Long-range axons have high metabolic demand and are vulnerable to injury, toxins, proteostatic and lysosomal stress, yet local energy failure as a driver of connectome disintegration is under-synthesized.
ocar.action: Yang, Park, and Lu, in Molecular Neurodegeneration (2023), review axonal energy metabolism across axon initial segments, myelinated segments, and presynaptic arbors, NAD+ homeostasis, and perturbations in aging and NDAs (AD, PD, HD, ALS).
ocar.resolution: They argue that metabolically expensive, long-range axons in topological hubs are innately vulnerable, that local bioenergetic dysregulation can precede frank degeneration, and that NAD+ imbalance, network hyperactivity, and glial pathology can exaggerate deficits in a still-asymptomatic phase. They call for metabolically oriented neuroprotection and for tests of causal links among metabolic vulnerability, axonopathy, amyloid/tau pathology, and cognition.
ocar.future_work: Interventional strategies to normalize bioenergetics in NDA models are encouraged; this article is a review, not a trial.

summaries.beginner: The long cables of the brain are energy-hungry, and in aging and diseases such as Alzheimer’s they often fail first. This review explains how axons make and use fuel, and why the most connected brain regions may be the most metabolically at risk.
summaries.intermediate: Yang, Park, and Lu (Molecular Neurodegeneration, 2023) review axonal bioenergetics in aging and neurodegenerative diseases. They link human glucose hypometabolism to disintegration of long-range, hub-like connections, then survey energy supply in the axon initial segment, myelinated internodes, and presynaptic boutons, including glial support. A second focus is NAD+ biosynthesis, recycling, and consumption. They argue that innate metabolic vulnerability of the connectome is worsened by NAD+ disruption, hyperactivity, and glia, and they advocate metabolically oriented neuroprotection research.
summaries.advanced: This is a review; disease mechanisms are literature synthesis. The selected extract’s end is abbreviations and declarations (no competing interests; accepted 8 June 2023). Catalog stages (segmentation, graph_analysis) do not describe the paper. Causal chains among metabolism, axonopathy, and proteinopathy are posed as future tests.

plain_language_summary: The long cables of the brain are energy-hungry, and in aging and diseases such as Alzheimer’s they often fail first. This review explains how axons make and use fuel, and why the most connected brain regions may be the most metabolically at risk.
